claim: Planned comparisons revealed no significant between-group differences at either the week 5 or week 9 follow-up timepoints, including all subscales, except that in the HH group the paired associates scores decreased (PL vs HH adjusted treatment difference: −0.55 ± 0.43, p<0.01**).

claim: Effect sizes, as quantified by Cohen's d, remained small (d < 0.3) on all scales, with the exception of the drug intensity VAS (d = 0.58).

evidence: This claim is supported by effect size calculations from the study's data.

claim: Among post-acute measures, condition was significant only on the anxiety measure (STAIT; −1.4 ± 1.3, p=0.03*).
source: Among post-acute measures, condition was significant only on the anxiety measure (STAIT; −1.4 ± 1.3, p=0.03*), meaning that anxiety was reduced at the end of microdose weeks compared with placebo weeks, see Table 2 for details on both acute and post-acute outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study's data.

claim: Anxiety was reduced at the end of microdose weeks compared with placebo weeks.
source: Among post-acute measures, condition was significant only on the anxiety measure (STAIT; −1.4 ± 1.3, p=0.03*), meaning that anxiety was reduced at the end of microdose weeks compared with placebo weeks, see Table 2 for details on both acute and post-acute outcomes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results.

claim: When the guess component was added to the models, condition (PL vs. MD) was no longer significant for any scale, except for acute drug intensity VAS (adjusted mean difference ±95% CI: 3.4 ± 2.0; p<0.001***).
source: Next, the acute and post-acute results were re-analyzed with the addition of guess into the models. Condition (PL vs. MD) was no longer significant for any scale, except for acute drug intensity VAS (adjusted mean difference ±95% CI: 3.4 ± 2.0; p<0.001***), which increased under MD (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis with guess as a covariate.

claim: The guess*condition interaction term was non-significant for all scales, except for drug intensity (p<0.01**).
source: The guess*condition interaction term was non-significant for all scales, except for drug intensity (p<0.01**).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of interaction effects.

claim: For self-reported outcomes, no significant differences were found between microdose and placebo conditions with fixed guess (condition/guess: PL/PL vs. MD/PL and PL/MD vs. MD/MD comparisons), except for acute drug intensity visual analogue scale, which was higher when microdose was taken (adj. mean difference ±95% CI; 7.3 ± 3.1, p<0.001***).
source: For self-reported outcomes, no significant differences were found between microdose and placebo conditions with fixed guess (condition/guess: PL/PL vs. MD/PL and PL/MD vs. MD/MD comparisons), except for acute drug intensity visual analogue scale, which was higher when microdose was taken (adj. mean difference ±95% CI; 7.3 ± 3.1, p<0.001***).
evidence: This claim is supported by stratified analysis of the study's data.

claim: When drug condition was fixed (condition/guess: PL/PL vs. PL/MD and MD/PL vs. MD/MD comparisons), significant differences were found in 21 of the 22 comparisons (=2*conditions*(4*post-acute+7*acute scales)), all favoring MD guess.
source: Conversely, when drug condition was fixed (condition/guess: PL/PL vs. PL/MD and MD/PL vs. MD/MD comparisons), significant differences were found in 21 of the 22 comparisons (=2*conditions*(4*post-acute+7*acute scales)), all favoring MD guess.
evidence: This claim is supported by stratified analysis of the study's data.

claim: Scores are significantly better when the participant believed they had taken a microdose irrespective of what was actually taken.
source: These findings suggest that scores are significantly better when the participant believed they had taken a microdose irrespective of what was actually taken.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the stratified analysis results.

claim: Taking an actual microdose was only associated with a significant difference in the drug intensity scale.
source: Taking an actual microdose was only associated with a significant difference in the drug intensity scale.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the stratified analysis results.

claim: Break blind rate, defined as the proportion of correct capsule guesses, was 0.72 ± 0.18 (M ± SD).
source: Break blind rate, defined as the proportion of correct capsule guesses (see section Blind breaking and collection of guess data for details), was 0.72 ± 0.18 (M ± SD).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study's data.

claim: Specificity (true negative rate: ratio of true placebo guesses to all placebo guesses) was 0.82 ± 0.16.
source: Specificity (true negative rate: ratio of true placebo guesses to all placebo guesses) was 0.82 ± 0.16, noticeably higher than sensitivity (true positive rate: ratio of true microdose guesses to all microdose guesses) 0.45 ± 0.30, meaning that placebo capsules were guessed correctly at a higher rate than microdoses.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study's data.

claim: Sensitivity (true positive rate: ratio of true microdose guesses to all microdose guesses) was 0.45 ± 0.30.
source: Specificity (true negative rate: ratio of true placebo guesses to all placebo guesses) was 0.82 ± 0.16, noticeably higher than sensitivity (true positive rate: ratio of true microdose guesses to all microdose guesses) 0.45 ± 0.30, meaning that placebo capsules were guessed correctly at a higher rate than microdoses.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study's data.

claim: Placebo capsules were guessed correctly at a higher rate than microdoses.
source: Specificity (true negative rate: ratio of true placebo guesses to all placebo guesses) was 0.82 ± 0.16, noticeably higher than sensitivity (true positive rate: ratio of true microdose guesses to all microdose guesses) 0.45 ± 0.30, meaning that placebo capsules were guessed correctly at a higher rate than microdoses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the specificity and sensitivity data.

claim: Based on knowledge of the ratio of PL/MD capsules (3/1) in the envelopes, a 'random guesser' would have a break blind rate of 0.62 with 0.75 specificity and 0.25 sensitivity.
source: Based on knowledge of the ratio of PL/MD capsules (3/1) in the envelopes, which is evident to participants when they prepare the capsules, a 'random guesser' would have a break blind rate of 0.62 with 0.75 specificity and 0.25 sensitivity.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the study design.

claim: The high sensitivity exhibited by participants (0.46 vs. the random guesser's 0.25) suggests that the higher than random break blind rate is mostly due to superior ability to identify microdoses.
source: The high sensitivity exhibited by participants (0.46 vs. the random guesser's 0.25) suggests that the higher than random break blind rate is mostly due to superior ability to identify microdoses, see Appendix 1—table 1 for details.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing observed and expected sensitivity.

claim: Break blind rate was positively associated with reported microdose dose (F(1, 237)=7.4, p<0.01**).
source: Break blind rate was positively associated with reported microdose dose (F(1, 237)=7.4, p<0.01**), meaning that the higher the dose was, the more likely participants guessed their daily condition correctly.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the relationship between dose and blind breaking.

claim: The higher the dose was, the more likely participants guessed their daily condition correctly.
source: Break blind rate was positively associated with reported microdose dose (F(1, 237)=7.4, p<0.01**), meaning that the higher the dose was, the more likely participants guessed their daily condition correctly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical association.

claim: The estimated 'detection threshold', that is, the dose above which participants guess significantly better than random, was 12 µg.
source: The estimated 'detection threshold', that is, the dose above which participants guess significantly better than random, was 12 µg.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the dose-blind breaking relationship.

claim: This study is the first one to use a self-blinding methodology.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first one to use a self-blinding methodology, the first placebo-controlled investigation of the accumulative effects of repeated microdosing, and the largest placebo-controlled psychedelic study to-date.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's methodology.

claim: This study is the first placebo-controlled investigation of the accumulative effects of repeated microdosing.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first one to use a self-blinding methodology, the first placebo-controlled investigation of the accumulative effects of repeated microdosing, and the largest placebo-controlled psychedelic study to-date.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's focus.

claim: Results confirmed the psychological benefits reported by anecdotes and observational, uncontrolled studies when looking at changes over time from baseline to week 5 in the microdose group alone.
source: When looking at changes over time from baseline to week 5 (accumulative outcomes) in the microdose group alone, results confirmed the psychological benefits reported by anecdotes (Fadiman and Krob, 2017) and observational, uncontrolled studies (Anderson et al., 2019; Polito and Stevenson, 2019; Prochazkova et al., 2018): significant improvements were observed in the domains of well-being, mindfulness, life satisfaction, and paranoia.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the within-group results in relation to prior literature.

claim: Significant improvements were observed in the domains of well-being, mindfulness, life satisfaction, and paranoia in the microdose group from baseline to week 5.
source: When looking at changes over time from baseline to week 5 (accumulative outcomes) in the microdose group alone, results confirmed the psychological benefits reported by anecdotes (Fadiman and Krob, 2017) and observational, uncontrolled studies (Anderson et al., 2019; Polito and Stevenson, 2019; Prochazkova et al., 2018): significant improvements were observed in the domains of well-being, mindfulness, life satisfaction, and paranoia.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study's data.

claim: The microdose group did not improve from baseline to week 5 on cognitive tests.
source: On the cognitive tests, which are less subjective than the self-reported psychological outcomes, the microdose group did not even improve from baseline to week 5 and the between-groups comparisons were not significant either.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study's data.

claim: The between-groups comparisons on cognitive tests were not significant.
source: On the cognitive tests, which are less subjective than the self-reported psychological outcomes, the microdose group did not even improve from baseline to week 5 and the between-groups comparisons were not significant either.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study's data.

claim: The study validates the positive anecdotal reports about the psychological benefits of microdosing (significant improvements from baseline in a broad range of psychological measures).
source: Thus, our study validates the positive anecdotal reports about the psychological benefits of microdosing (significant improvements from baseline in a broad range of psychological measures); however, our results also suggest that these improvements are not due to the pharmacological action of microdosing, but are rather explained by the placebo effect (lack of significant between-groups differences).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in relation to anecdotal reports.

claim: The improvements observed in microdosing are not due to the pharmacological action of microdosing, but are rather explained by the placebo effect (lack of significant between-groups differences).
source: Thus, our study validates the positive anecdotal reports about the psychological benefits of microdosing (significant improvements from baseline in a broad range of psychological measures); however, our results also suggest that these improvements are not due to the pharmacological action of microdosing, but are rather explained by the placebo effect (lack of significant between-groups differences).
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the lack of between-group differences.

claim: The clinical and practical value of the small effects observed on acute and post-acute outcomes is debatable.
source: Effect sizes were small on all scales (Cohen's d < 0.3 except drug intensity); thus, the clinical and practical value of these effects is debatable.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the clinical significance of small effect sizes.

claim: The addition of the guess variable to the models may undermine the statistical significance of the condition effect due to collinearity between condition and guess.
source: It can be argued that the addition of the guess variable to the models may undermine the statistical significance of the condition effect due to collinearity between condition and guess.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration about potential confounding.

claim: Neither CPS nor any cognitive subtask were significantly different under either guess or drug conditions.
source: Importantly, neither CPS nor any cognitive subtask, the non-self-rated outcomes where beliefs and subjective feelings are likely to be less influential, were significantly different under either guess or drug conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of cognitive outcomes.

claim: The actual content of capsules did not determine differences between the conditions, but beliefs about their content did.
source: In summary, these results strongly suggest that the actual content of capsules did not determine differences between the conditions, but beliefs about their content did.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the stratified analysis results.

claim: Participants guessed their capsules correctly in 72% of the cases.
source: An important observation was that participants guessed their capsules correctly in 72% of the cases.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study's data.

claim: The break blind rate was higher than random (random: 63% vs. participants: 72%).
source: This break blind rate was higher than random (random: 63% vs. participants: 72%), but not as high as reported in antidepressant studies (around 80%) (Chen et al., 2011; Kirsch, 2019; Rabkin et al., 1986).
evidence: This is a comparison of observed break blind rate to expected and literature values.

claim: The break blind rate was not as high as reported in antidepressant studies (around 80%).
source: This break blind rate was higher than random (random: 63% vs. participants: 72%), but not as high as reported in antidepressant studies (around 80%) (Chen et al., 2011; Kirsch, 2019; Rabkin et al., 1986).
evidence: This is a comparison to literature values supported by citations.

claim: It is known from a variety of clinical studies that higher break blind rate is associated with larger between-conditions effect-sizes (where placebo is the control condition).
source: It is known from a variety of clinical studies that higher break blind rate is associated with larger between-conditions effect-sizes (where placebo is the control condition) (Baethge et al., 2013; Berna et al., 2017; Laferton et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: This relationship between break blind rate and effect size is explained by non-specific treatment factors such as expectation of a benefit and investigator alliance.
source: This relationship is explained by non-specific treatment factors such as expectation of a benefit (Bausell, 2009) and investigator alliance (Chatoor and Kurpnick, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The influence of non-specific treatment factors is likely to be large for the present study, because of highly positive expectations and favorable attitudes toward psychedelics.
source: The influence of such factors is likely to be large for the present study, because of highly positive expectations and favorable attitudes toward psychedelics, see attitude analysis in the Appendix.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's demographic data and general knowledge.

claim: The observed 'significant' acute and post-acute effects may be an artifact of the combination of break blinds and expected benefits.
source: These factors together suggest that the observed 'significant' acute and post-acute effects may be an artifact of the combination of break blinds and expected benefits.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: The acute and post-acute results observed could be understood as the difference between the expected benefits when a microdose is perceived versus the absence of expected benefits when placebo is perceived.
source: The acute and post-acute results observed could be understood as the difference between the expected benefits when a microdose is perceived (i.e. guessed by participants) versus the absence of expected benefits when placebo is perceived.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism behind the results.

claim: This difference in expectations could be mistaken for a 'real' drug effect in any study where blinding integrity is not considered during analysis.
source: This difference in expectations could be mistaken for a 'real' drug effect in any study where blinding integrity is not considered during analysis.
evidence: This is a general methodological inference about the importance of assessing blinding.

claim: One prediction for future microdose studies with a similarly pro-psychedelics sample is that they may observe larger effects when break blind rate is higher, or conversely, smaller effects when break blind rate is lower.
source: If this explanation is correct, one prediction for future microdose studies with a similarly pro-psychedelics sample is that they may observe larger effects when break blind rate is higher, or conversely, smaller effects when break blind rate is lower.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction for future research.

claim: Drug intensity was the only outcome that remained significant even after adjusting for guess (3.4 ± 2.0; p<0.001***).
source: What factors account for the blind breaking? Drug intensity was the only outcome that remained significant even after adjusting for guess (3.4 ± 2.0; p<0.001***).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis with guess adjustment.

claim: Increased drug intensity mostly manifested as body and perceptual sensations.
source: This increased drug intensity mostly manifested as body and perceptual sensations, see Blind breaking cues in Appendix 1 for details.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the study's data.

claim: In most cases blind breaking induced clinically irrelevant side effects, rather than deduced from improvements of outcome variables.
source: This finding suggests that in most cases blind breaking induced clinically irrelevant side effects, rather than deduced from improvements of outcome variables.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of blind breaking.

claim: According to the data, the threshold LSD dose where participants guess better than random is 12 µg, which is in line with the 13 µg threshold dose estimated by a recent dose controlled study.
source: We note that according to our data the threshold LSD dose where participants guess better than random is 12 µg, see Figure 4, which is in line with the 13 µg threshold dose estimated by a recent dose controlled study (Bershad et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is a comparison of the study's finding to a cited study.

claim: The current study was designed to protect blinding integrity by including placebos for the microdose group as well, administering the microdose capsules on different days of the week and by including the half-half group.
source: It is worth noting that the current study was designed to protect blinding integrity by including placebos for the microdose group as well, administering the microdose capsules on different days of the week and by including the half-half group.
evidence: This is a description of the study's design features.

claim: The 3-arm design can be seen as a strength in this regard, adding ambiguity and thus strengthening blinding.
source: The 3-arm design can be seen as a strength in this regard, adding ambiguity and thus strengthening blinding.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the study design.

claim: The present part-controlled, part-observational design yields data superior to conventional observational data (inclusion of placebo control), but inferior to controlled clinical trial data (incomplete control over recruitment, screening, assessment, drug administration, etc.).
source: It is our view that the present part-controlled, part-observational design yields data superior to conventional observational data (inclusion of placebo control), but inferior to controlled clinical trial data (incomplete control over recruitment, screening, assessment, drug administration, etc.).
evidence: This is an assessment of the study's methodological strengths and limitations.

claim: This study has greater ecological validity than would a fully controlled lab study.
source: This study does, however, have greater ecological validity than would a fully controlled lab study.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the naturalistic design.

claim: A key limitation of the present study is the lack of verification of the nature, purity, and dosage of the psychedelic substance used for microdosing.
source: A key limitation of the present study is the lack of verification of the nature, purity, and dosage of the psychedelic substance used for microdosing.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a methodological limitation.

claim: According to the Energy Control's drug checking service (Barcelona), LSD blotter adulteration rates were low during the period when the study was running: in both 2018 and 2019 blotters sold as LSD contained LSD only in 90% (n = 735) of tested samples.
source: According to the Energy Control's drug checking service (Barcelona), LSD blotter adulteration rates were low during the period when our study was running: in both 2018 and 2019 blotters sold as LSD contained LSD only in 90% (n = 735) of tested samples [personal communication with M. Ventrua from EC, June 2020].
evidence: This claim is supported by external data from a drug checking service.

claim: The positive relationship between dose and blind breaking and that the threshold dose for psychoactivity was consistent with a recent controlled study (12 µg vs 13 µg) provide some reassurance about substance quality.
source: The exact quantity of active ingredient within a given microdose cannot be known with certainty; however, the positive relationship between dose and blind breaking (Figure 4) and that the threshold dose for psychoactivity was consistent with a recent controlled study (12 µg vs 13 µg; Bershad et al., 2019a) provide some reassurance.
evidence: This is an inference about substance quality based on dose-response relationships.

claim: The results should not be understood as clinical evidence, rather they are representative of 'real life microdosing'.
source: Nonetheless, our results should be not understood as clinical evidence, rather they are representative of 'real life microdosing'.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation and generalizability of the findings.

claim: The study could not confirm whether participants followed accurately the self-blinding procedure.
source: We could not confirm whether participants followed accurately the self-blinding procedure.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a methodological limitation.

claim: Three individuals reported following an invalid sequence of weeks, but these individuals did their setups together, all committing the same mistake (1.3% error rate).
source: Three individuals reported following an invalid sequence of weeks, but these individuals did their setups together, all committing the same mistake (1.3% error rate).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding about protocol adherence.

claim: The study had no way of confirming whether the capsules were taken as instructed during the dose period.
source: Furthermore, we had no way of confirming whether the capsules were taken as instructed during the dose period.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a methodological limitation.

claim: The stratification analysis does not allow for a strict determination of a causal relationship between guess and outcome, because guess was recorded after completion of assessments.
source: Our stratification analysis does not allow for a strict determination of a causal relationship between guess and outcome, because guess was recorded after completion of assessments, guess was last question during test sessions.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a methodological limitation regarding causal inference.

claim: After closing the study, a survey was conducted among participants, where 86% (n = 166) responded that 'I was thinking about whether I took a microdose or placebo even before I was asked to guess'.
source: After closing the study, a survey was conducted among participants, where 86% (n = 166) responded that "I was thinking about whether I took a microdose or placebo even before I was asked to guess" (opposed to "I was not thinking about whether I took a microdose or placebo, except when I was asked to guess"), making a causal interpretation more likely.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from a post-study survey.

claim: The order of guess collection is consistent with previous work in psychiatric studies.
source: We note that the order we chose is consistent with previous work in psychiatric studies (Baethge et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2011; Rabkin et al., 1986); had the guesses been requested prior to the assessments, it could have primed responses.
evidence: This is a methodological justification supported by citations.

claim: Had the guesses been requested prior to the assessments, it could have primed responses.
source: We note that the order we chose is consistent with previous work in psychiatric studies (Baethge et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2011; Rabkin et al., 1986); had the guesses been requested prior to the assessments, it could have primed responses.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential methodological confounding.

claim: The study cannot rule out that performance during the assessments influenced the guess.
source: Also, we cannot rule out that performance during the assessments influenced the guess.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a potential confound.

claim: The lack of any feedback from the assessments mitigates the risk that performance influenced guess.
source: However, the lack of any feedback from the assessments mitigates this risk.
evidence: This is an inference about a design feature that reduces confounding.

claim: Most participants reported to break blind due to body and perceptual sensations, rather than improved outcomes.
source: Most participants reported to break blind due to body and perceptual sensations, rather than improved outcomes, see Blind breaking cues in the Appendix for details.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the study's data.

claim: The study cannot rule out the possibility that a study in a clinical population would yield more promising results.
source: We cannot rule out the possibility that a study in a clinical population would yield more promising results.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about generalizability.

claim: In the present healthy sample, where well-being scores are high at baseline, there is less scope for potential improvements, which could have prevented the observation of placebo-microdose differences.
source: In the present healthy sample, where well-being scores are high at baseline, there is less scope for potential improvements, which could have prevented the observation of placebo-microdose differences.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of between-group differences.

claim: Results in the pseudo-depression subsamples were entirely consistent with those from the complete sample: there were no significant differences between conditions for any of the accumulative outcomes.
source: We conducted two post-hoc analysis for two selective pseudo-depression subsamples: participants with the lowest 25% baseline well-being scores and those with the highest 25% baseline neuroticism scores (Ryff and Keyes, 1995; Wood and Joseph, 2010). Results in these subsamples were entirely consistent with those from the complete sample: there were no significant differences between conditions for any of the accumulative outcomes
evidence: This claim is supported by post-hoc subgroup analysis.

claim: Although not designed as a clinical study, data from this opportunistic naturalistic study do not provide support for clinical effects of microdosing.
source: Thus, although not designed as a clinical study, data from this opportunistic naturalistic study do not provide support for clinical effects of microdosing.

source: Important lessons can be taken from the current study for the design of future microdosing trials.
